definition: A regulatory system that caps total allowable output of a pollutant (e.g., carbon dioxide) and requires every producer of that pollutant to hold a tradable license/permit covering their production; licenses can be freely bought and sold, so the market — not a regulator — sets the price of compliance. It is one of the two main tools governments have used to limit pollution (the other being a direct emissions tax), and it is the only one of the two that creates an actual trading market, since it issues tradable licenses rather than simply pricing emissions.
core_idea: By fixing the total quantity of allowed pollution and letting participants trade licenses within that cap, low-cost abaters can profit by cutting pollution and selling surplus licenses while high-cost abaters buy licenses to keep polluting — so the market, rather than a regulator, determines who reduces emissions first and pushes the cheapest reductions to happen first.
key_points: Taxes and cap-and-trade are described as the two most popular/common ways governments try to limit pollution; only cap-and-trade produces a genuine trading market, because it creates a tradable license/permit rather than simply pricing emissions.
A hard cap guarantees pollution stays below a defined level, unlike a tax, which only changes incentives; total emissions volume is fixed by the cap while permit price floats with supply and demand.
Every producer of the regulated substance must hold a license for their production; licenses can be freely bought and sold.

Tradability lets low-cost abaters profit by cutting pollution and selling surplus licenses to high-cost abaters who buy licenses to keep polluting — the market, not a regulator, determines who reduces emissions first.
Regulators can tighten the system over time by shrinking the total number of licenses issued, forcing further reductions starting with the cheapest ones.
The two central design problems for any cap-and-trade system are: how to allocate/distribute the initial licenses, and how to enforce compliance.
Government is typically revenue-neutral under cap-and-trade (it doesn't profit from the system), unlike a tax.
Trades are private company-to-company exchanges of goods (cash for permits) and can cross country borders and currencies without government intermediation.
Companies retain flexibility to either install cleaner technology or purchase emissions credits, whichever is cheaper for them.
Cap-and-trade creates a new class of tradable property/instrument (emissions rights/licenses/credits) where none previously existed as an asset class.

Advantages attributed to cap-and-trade over a tax: total pollution is well known in advance because of the cap; since compliance can be achieved globally via trading, there's no incentive for companies to relocate factories from high-tax to low-tax regions; it is broadly applicable across countries and different greenhouse gas types; unlike a tax system, which needs periodic legislative adjustment, a trading system self-adjusts to changing economic conditions.
Cap-and-trade underpins the Kyoto Protocol's international/national emissions allocation structure and real-world Kyoto-conforming emissions trading markets.

Comprehensive tracking of all CO2 emissions is impossible, and even if possible would be too complex to trade (e.g., a system can't realistically apply to something like a person jogging), so emissions trading markets must selectively choose which CO2 sources to restrict — most carbon trading focuses on fossil-fuel combustion.

Because only some emitters are capped, actions that lower measured emissions in the capped sector can raise true total emissions (e.g., shutting down a power-plant-powered commuter railroad reduces the capped power plant's emissions on paper but pushes former rail commuters into cars, raising overall regional emissions) — a general 'funny accounting' risk whenever offset/credit creation spans sources that aren't uniformly capped.

Carbon taxes and cap-and-trade systems commonly coexist rather than being mutually exclusive; taxes can be applied universally with minimal administration (e.g., a fuel surcharge is simpler than verifying emissions-credit ownership), and tax revenue can be reinvested locally, whereas cap-and-trade cash can transfer to a carbon sink in a different jurisdiction.
relationships: Contrasted with carbon taxes as the other main pollution-limiting policy tool.
Cap-and-trade licenses/permits function like tradable commodities, similar to other emissions permits.
Underpins the Kyoto Protocol's international/national emissions allocation structure and Kyoto-conforming emissions trading markets.
Related to carbon dioxide emissions and coal-fired generation economics.
The narrow-scope limitation of cap-and-trade (only some sources capped) is the root cause of the accounting-gaming risk (uncapped-sector leakage).
Contrasts with carbon taxes on cash-flow and administrative grounds (domestic tax revenue vs. cross-jurisdiction permit cash flow).
trading_implications: Cap-and-trade licenses are themselves a financial instrument that can be bought, sold, and used to profit from switching to cleaner technology — a new tradable asset class that did not previously exist.
Creates an arbitrage-like opportunity: entities with cheap abatement technology can generate income by selling excess licenses rather than using them.
Permit price is variable, driven by supply and demand plus macro factors like interest rates and FX rates, unlike a fixed tax cost.
Permit markets can dynamically reallocate the location of emissions cuts in response to interest rates, FX rates, and other economic stimuli, since it doesn't matter where the physical cuts occur.
Only facilities/sectors explicitly brought into scope face compliance obligations; large swaths of real-world emissions sit outside any market.
caveats: The two central design problems for any cap-and-trade system — how to allocate the initial licenses, and how to enforce compliance — are unresolved by the basic mechanism itself.

Comprehensive tracking of all CO2-producing activity is impossible (and would be too complex to trade even if possible), so schemes must selectively choose which sources to cap; most carbon trading focuses on fossil-fuel combustion, leaving many real-world emissions sources outside any market.

Narrow scope creates an accounting-gaming risk: reducing measured emissions in the capped sector can raise true total emissions if it pushes activity into an uncapped sector (e.g., the commuter-rail-to-car example).

Carbon taxes and cap-and-trade are not mutually exclusive and commonly coexist; a domestic energy tax is simpler to administer universally, while an international carbon tax remains unlikely because countries favor tax schemes that levy costs on other countries while benefiting themselves.
